title: Inference backlog erosion and operational safeguards for GPU exhaustion incident
creator: Aisha Morgan
description: Summary: During a hosted API capacity event on 2025-02-12 we observed a rapidly growing inference backlog that overwhelmed multiple GPU pools, causing sustained elevated latencies, throttling, and several customer 5xxs. Root cause analysis shows this was a combination of (1) a high-concurrency tenant spike executing many short chat requests with large prefix reuse, (2) an overly aggressive prefetch/pipelining config that amplified queue arrival bursts, and (3) autoscaler hysteresis and scale-up cadence that lagged the growth window. These factors combined to cause 'backlog erosion' — a pathological mode where queued requests repeatedly invalidate KV caches and prevent efficient packing, which in turn increased per-token GPU time and delayed autoscaler trigger signals.
acceptance_criteria: Per-tenant queue-length and kv-hit-rate metrics are emitted and visible in Grafana
A soft per-tenant admission cap (default 200 concurrent requests) is enforced with documented override process
Autoscaler hysteresis tuned and validated in staging to reduce time-to-scale by 30% without oscillation
Emergency capacity pool config and automated failover tested end-to-end
Runbook updated with ‘backlog erosion’ detection and mitigation steps and playbook owner assigned

rollout_plan: Canary 1: apply admission cap + slow-start to 1 host group (low-traffic region) for 24h
Canary 2: expand to 20% of fleet for 48h and monitor kv-hit-rate and latencies
Full rollout: 100% after 72h of stable telemetry and no increase in client errors
Rollback: revert admission cap at host-group level and divert traffic to emergency pool if average latency increases by >20% post-change
retrospective_notes: Key lessons: (1) Short, high-concurrency bursts are a first-class failure mode and demand different autoscaler primitives than steady growth. (2) KV cache effectiveness is a second-order control lever that materially changes per-token cost and scale triggers. (3) Observability gaps (no per-tenant queue metrics) delayed diagnosis. We will treat backlog erosion as a class of incident to be instrumented and trained on in future incident drills.
